strengths: Introduces a simple and practical extension to MoE by making expert hidden dimensions slimmable via nested subnetworks, adding a new axis of conditional computation (expert capacity) on top of expert selection.

The proposed multi-width pretraining recipe is straightforward to integrate with standard MoE training (top-k routing, load balancing, router z-loss), and the training-dynamics results suggest stable optimization across widths.

The inference-time width allocation framework is flexible: it supports uniform widths, router-probability-conditioned widths, and a lightweight calibration method for learning the sharpness parameter gamma under a compute budget.
The TTT procedure is low-dimensional (shared or layer-wise scalars) and keeps all model weights frozen, making it cheap to apply at deployment time.
Experiments cover multiple small-scale GPT models, routing configurations, and token budgets, and the TTT variant often improves the perplexity-compute Pareto frontier over uniform-width MoSE.
The paper includes a limitations section acknowledging the small-scale setting and the open question of post-training adaptation.
weaknesses: Training compute is not controlled: MoSE performs two forward/backward passes per iteration (full width plus a random width), so at the same token/iteration budget it receives roughly 2x the training FLOPs of the standard MoE baseline. The central claim that MoSE matches or improves MoE at full width may therefore be confounded by extra training compute/regularization rather than architectural benefit.

The efficiency claims are supported only by theoretical MFLOPs per token. There are no wall-clock latency, throughput, or hardware-utilization measurements, even though variable expert widths can lead to poor GPU efficiency, padding, load imbalance, and routing overhead. The title and introduction's emphasis on efficiency/latency is thus not fully substantiated.

The 'test-time training' method optimizes only a scalar or layer-wise sharpness parameter on a small calibration stream. No comparison is made to a simple grid search or validation-tuned fixed gamma under the same calibration budget, so it is unclear whether learned gamma provides value beyond standard hyperparameter tuning.

The paper does not empirically compare against closely related elastic MoE or adaptive-compute baselines (e.g., RoE, Elastic MoE, MatFormer, LLM-Flex, early-exit, Mixture-of-Depths), despite claiming Pareto-frontier improvements. This makes the originality and relative significance hard to assess.

The empirical evaluation is limited to small GPT models (55M-1B) trained on OpenWebText for 3B-15B tokens, with zero-shot evaluation only on LAMBADA and WSC. This is far from the 'large language model' framing, and no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; small WSC/LAMBADA accuracy differences could easily be noise.

Several methodological details are unclear or inconsistent: how auxiliary losses are applied across the two width passes, exactly how training widths are sampled/discretized, how FLOPs are counted, and whether the Table 1 TTT results at maximum budget Γ=|S(x)| actually use fewer FLOPs than full-width MoE. Equation 3 also has inconsistent notation (w_r vs w_m), and the reference list contains several citation/year errors.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, training compute is not reported, and key TTT details (per-budget calibration, layer-wise gamma initialization, optimizer schedule) are only partially specified.

strengths: The MoSE formulation is clear and technically plausible: it extends MoE by making each expert FFN's intermediate dimension slimmable via nested slicing, allowing execution at variable widths.
The training recipe is simple: multi-width training with full width and one random width, combined with standard load-balancing and router z-loss, requiring no changes to standard MoE pipelines.

The inference-time width allocation strategies are well motivated and include uniform width, router-probability-conditioned widths, and a lightweight test-time training procedure to learn a sharpness parameter gamma.

The empirical study spans several model scales (55M, 322M, 1B), routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4), and token budgets (3B-15B), and evaluates language modeling perplexity plus zero-shot LAMBADA and WSC.
The appendix provides useful reproducibility details, including architecture hyperparameters, optimizer settings, slimmable width range, calibration procedure, and compute hardware.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges the small-scale nature of the experiments and leaves post-training adaptation as open future work.
weaknesses: Central claims are not adequately supported. Table 1 shows MoSE (w=1.0) sometimes underperforms MoE (e.g., GPT2-Small 15B: OpenWebText 31.26 vs 31.03, WikiText-103 121.50 vs 120.48), and reported gains are small and lack seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. WSC has only 273 examples, making differences noisy.

The Pareto-frontier comparison against standard MoE is weak. Standard MoE is mostly a single full-width point; the main curves compare MoSE (TTT) against uniform-width MoSE, which is an ablation of the proposed method. There is no comparison to standard MoE at reduced compute (e.g., fewer active experts k, smaller experts, or distillation) or to strong elastic MoE baselines such as EMoE, RoE, MatFormer, or LLamaFlex.

The scale is far from LLM scale. Experiments use GPT-2-like models up to 1B parameters and 3B-15B training tokens, while the abstract and introduction motivate the work for LLMs. It is unclear whether the marginal gains would persist at modern MoE scales.

The 'fixed budget' width assignment is not strictly enforced. After w_i = Gamma * q_i, the projection/clipping to [w_min, w_max] without renormalization can make the actual total width exceed or fall below Gamma. This can confound compute-performance comparisons and undermines the budgeted allocation claim.

Test-time training (TTT) is insufficiently analyzed. The calibration cost (50 batches) is not included in the reported MFLOPs, it is not specified whether calibration data is disjoint from evaluation data for OpenWebText, and transferability is only tested on LAMBADA. The learned gamma may be exploiting in-domain calibration rather than providing a general compute-aware mapping.

Important ablations are missing: no study of how many widths to sample during pretraining (they use only full + one random width; no sandwich rule or min-width training), no analysis of slicing/order effects, no comparison against random or oracle width allocation, and no breakdown of the marginal benefit of TTT versus simply tuning a fixed gamma.

Originality is incremental. The core idea combines MoE with slimmable/nested networks, and the main new component is learning a scalar (or layer-wise) sharpness parameter at test time. The paper acknowledges closely related elastic MoE work but does not empirically compare against it.

Presentation and reproducibility have gaps. Exact inference FLOPs are not reported in Table 1 despite the asterisk claim of lower FLOPs; figures are small and hard to read; some references have duplicate/incorrect entries; and no code or checkpoints are provided.
The limitations discussion is honest but does not address the most critical experimental gaps: lack of strong baselines, budget enforcement, statistical rigor, and scale.

strengths: Introduces a novel and natural extension of MoE by combining slimmable/nested-width experts with sparse routing, enabling conditional computation over both expert selection and expert capacity.
The proposed training recipe is simple, stable, and compatible with standard MoE pipelines; multi-width training samples full width plus a random width, avoiding major architectural changes.

The inference-time strategies, especially the lightweight test-time training of the sharpness parameter gamma, are creative and low-dimensional, enabling budget-aware width allocation without updating pretrained weights.

Experiments across multiple model scales (GPT2-Small/Standard/Medium), routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4), and token budgets (3B-15B) show consistent Pareto-frontier improvements over uniform-width MoSE and standard MoE.

The paper provides useful analyses, including training dynamics across widths, FLOPs breakdown showing MoE dominates compute, learned gamma behavior under different budgets, and an ablation isolating the benefit of TTT over fixed normalized-probability width allocation.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed hyperparameters, model architectures, routing settings, and evaluation protocols in the appendix.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges that experiments are limited to small-scale models and that post-training instillation of slimmability remains open.
weaknesses: No empirical comparison is provided against closely related elastic MoE methods such as EMoE and RoE, despite these being discussed in related work; this weakens the claim that MoSE meaningfully advances the state of the art in elastic MoE inference.

The test-time training procedure for optimizing gamma is unclear when widths are discretized: if widths are projected to a discrete set, the language-modeling loss is piecewise constant in gamma, so gradients with respect to gamma are zero almost everywhere. The paper does not describe using continuous relaxation, straight-through estimators, finite differences, or other techniques to make this optimization well-defined.

Efficiency claims rely exclusively on theoretical MFLOPs per token. No wall-clock latency, throughput, or hardware measurements are reported, even though dynamic width slicing may not translate into proportional real-world speedups due to kernel inefficiencies and memory alignment issues.

The training overhead of MoSE is not quantified. MoSE runs the model twice per iteration (full width and random width), roughly doubling training compute relative to standard MoE, but the paper describes this as 'low overhead' without measuring or accounting for it in compute-matched comparisons.

Zero-shot evaluation results lack error bars or statistical significance tests. This is especially concerning for WSC, which has only 273 validation examples, and for LAMBADA accuracy, where differences between methods are small and occasionally non-monotonic.

The claim that MoSE 'matches or improves upon standard MoE at full width' is not consistently supported: in Table 1, some full-width MoSE perplexities are slightly worse than MoE (e.g., GPT2-Small 15B on OpenWebText and WikiText-103, GPT2-Standard 3B on WikiText-103).

The experimental scale is limited to GPT-2-style models up to 1B parameters trained on OpenWebText for at most 15B tokens. It remains unclear whether the approach scales to modern large language models or to more diverse pretraining data.

The TTT calibration stream is drawn from OpenWebText, the same domain as pretraining, which may inflate in-domain perplexity gains and complicates the interpretation of the 'zero-shot' downstream results. The paper should clarify that this is unsupervised in-domain adaptation, not purely zero-shot inference.

Several presentation and consistency issues reduce clarity: Section 3.1 states that 'all MoSE models are trained using uniform-width execution,' which contradicts the multi-width pretraining described in Section 2.3; there are also reference typos and duplicate citations.

The paper does not ablate key training choices such as the number of sampled widths per iteration, the minimum width w_min, the discretization step size, or the effect of training with more than two widths. This limits understanding of what drives the gains and how sensitive the method is to these hyperparameters.

The abstract claims 'significantly fewer FLOPs,' but the main text does not provide a concise table reporting FLOPs savings at matched perplexity; the evidence is mostly visual in Pareto plots, making it harder to assess the practical magnitude of the efficiency gains.

strengths: Originality/significance: MoSE cleanly combines slimmable/nested networks with sparse MoE to add an inference-time width axis, a natural and potentially useful extension of conditional computation in MoE.

Core training recipe is simple and stable: multi-width training with full width plus a random width, standard load-balancing loss, and router z-loss; training curves and routing diagnostics (CV, entropy, JS divergence) suggest no severe routing collapse.

Empirical breadth: experiments span GPT2-Small/Standard/Medium/Large, E8A2/E8A4/E16A4/E64A8/E128A8, OpenWebText/WikiText-103/LAMBADA/WSC/HellaSwag/PIQA/SIQA, plus CPT on DeepSeek-V2-Lite; reported Pareto shifts and FLOPs reductions are promising.

Useful ablations and transfer analyses: uniform-width, normalized-probability, and TTT inference modes; inference-time routing transfer; gamma transfer to LAMBADA; and appendix diagnostics on runtime and FLOPs breakdown.
Limitations and ethics: the paper acknowledges the lack of frontier-scale from-scratch training and discusses safety/robustness across widths.
weaknesses: Soundness/evidential confound: MoSE training uses two forward passes per step (full width plus sampled width), while the MoE baseline uses one. Full-width improvements may come from extra training compute/regularization rather than slimmability; no training-FLOPs-matched comparison is provided.

Missing baselines: despite discussing elastic MoE methods such as RoE and EMoE, the paper does not compare against them, nor against simpler alternatives such as MoE with smaller FFNs, variable top-k, pruning, or distillation. This makes it hard to establish that MoSE shifts the frontier beyond a standard MoE baseline.

Evaluation leakage concern: TTT calibrates gamma on OpenWebText and is then evaluated on OpenWebText perplexity; it is unclear whether the calibration split is disjoint from the held-out evaluation split. In-domain gains may be inflated by adapting to the evaluation distribution.

Unsupported full-width claim: Table 1 shows MoSE(w=1.0) worse than MoE in several cases, e.g. GPT2-Small 15B: 31.26 vs 31.03 OpenWebText PPL and 121.50 vs 120.48 WikiText; GPT2-Standard 3B WSC: 0.5128 vs 0.5201. This contradicts the claim that MoSE matches or improves standard MoE at full width.

Overstated TTT: the test-time training learns only a scalar, or per-layer scalar, sharpness gamma inside a fixed probability-to-width mapping. The abstract claim that it learns how to map router confidence/probabilities to expert widths suggests a much more general learned mapping than is implemented.

Practical efficiency uncertainty: per-token mixed widths create irregular computation. The paper reports FLOPs reductions, but wall-clock benefits depend on kernel implementation, grouping/padding, and memory-bound matmuls; runtime evidence is relegated to a brief appendix and not integrated into the main claims.

Reproducibility: the code link is blank, no seeds or error bars are reported, runs appear single-seed, calibration is only 50 batches x 6, WSC has only 273 examples, and the exact calibration split and whether test data are used for gamma tuning are not specified.

Presentation and notation issues: garbled placeholder text appears after Figure 1; notation is inconsistent (W_up vs W_sp, w_r vs w_m); references contain errors such as Cai et al. 2024 for 2020/2025 work and Grattafori typo; Figure 1 caption claims more experts contribute although the method still uses the same top-k selected experts.

Significance/validation gaps: the DeepSeek-V2-Lite CPT result is only a figure with no table, absolute numbers, or downstream zero-shot evaluation; downstream reasoning improvements in Table 2 are modest, single-seed, and not significance-tested.
Hyperparameter sensitivity is not studied: no sensitivity analysis for w_min, width discretization step, calibration size, gamma optimizer/learning rate, or compute budget.

Originality is incremental: the combination is intuitive, and the paper does not isolate why multi-width training helps at full width, e.g. as a regularizer, or compare to simple width-noise/dropout regularization.

strengths: The core idea—combining nested, slimmable expert widths with sparse MoE routing to add a second axis of conditional computation—is sensible and targets a genuinely underexplored dimension (expert capacity, not just expert selection).

The empirical scope is broad: multiple model scales (55M–2.5B), several routing regimes (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4, E64A8, E128A8), zero-shot benchmarks (LAMBADA, WSC, HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA), and continual pre-training adaptation on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B).

The training recipe (full width + one random width per step) is simple, and Figure 3 plus the routing diagnostics in Appendix B.5 support the claim that multi-width training does not destabilize routing.

The TTT mechanism for learning the sharpness parameter gamma is lightweight (a single scalar or one scalar per layer) and consistently dominates both uniform-width and normalized-probability allocation across the reported Pareto frontiers (Figures 4–9).
The paper is reasonably honest about limitations (no frontier-scale from-scratch training) and includes useful auxiliary analyses (FLOPs breakdown, runtime diagnostics, width-wise training dynamics).
weaknesses: No empirical comparison to the most directly relevant baselines the paper itself positions against (RoE and Elastic MoE/EMoE, discussed in Related Work). Without these, or a simple post-hoc width-pruning baseline on a standard MoE, it is unclear whether MoSE's gains come from the proposed mechanism or from generic width-robust training.

The headline compute savings (20–40% FLOPs at matched perplexity) rest on gamma calibrated on OpenWebText (Appendix A.1: 'We fix the calibration set to OpenWebText everywhere') while the primary perplexity evaluations are also on OpenWebText. This is a potential calibration/evaluation overlap that weakens the central evidence, even if the LAMBADA transfer results partially mitigate it.

The claim that MoSE 'matches or improves standard MoE at full width' is not well supported: in Table 1 (GPT2-Small, 15B, OpenWebText), MoSE (w=1.0) is worse than MoE (31.26 vs 31.03), and several other full-width deltas are within noise. The narrative overstates this.

Presentation quality is poor in places: Section 1.2 and Section 1.2.1 contain verbatim duplicated text; an entire paragraph ('For the real-world problem, we use the same model as the real-world problem...') is garbled; equation (3) writes 'w_r = 1.0' while the set is defined with m elements, and m(w) uses 4d inconsistently with the expert's 4d expansion. The code link in the abstract is empty.

The mechanism itself is largely an application of slimmable/nested-width training (Yu et al., 2019; Horvath et al., 2021; Kusupati et al., 2022) to MoE experts, and the TTT contribution reduces to fitting one scalar (or one scalar per layer). The conceptual novelty beyond this combination is limited.

The rationale for why test-time training of a single scalar gamma produces such consistent Pareto improvements is not theoretically justified, and the effect of the budget sweep Gamma and how gamma* is selected per budget is under-specified, making reproduction of the Pareto frontiers difficult.

Table 2 reports zero-shot gains for MoSE (TTT) at reduced FLOPs on GPT2-Medium, but these results are single-point comparisons without confidence intervals or seeds, and the accuracy jump (e.g., HellaSwag 0.335 to 0.385) is large for a small model and would benefit from variance estimates.

The 'more continuous spectrum of accuracy-compute tradeoffs' claim in the abstract is somewhat undermined by the discretization of widths to a 0.05 step (Appendix A.2), and by the fact that full-width performance is essentially on par with the MoE baseline.

strengths: Introduces MoSE, a simple and general extension of MoE with slimmable experts via nested widths, enabling conditional computation over expert capacity as well as expert selection.

Provides a stable multi-width training recipe that combines full-width and sampled-width passes with standard MoE objectives, and shows convergence and full-width parity across GPT2 scales and routing regimes.

Conducts broad experiments: GPT2-Small/Standard/Medium/Large, E8A2/E8A4/E16A4/E64A8/E128A8, OpenWebText/WikiText-103, zero-shot LAMBADA/WSC/HellaSwag/PIQA/SIQA, and continual-pretraining adaptation on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B).

Demonstrates that the proposed lightweight test-time calibration of the sharpness parameter gamma improves compute-quality trade-offs over uniform-width execution and normalized-probability allocation, with transfer to LAMBADA.
Discusses practical deployment regimes (full pretraining vs continual pretraining) and includes an honest limitations section noting the lack of frontier-scale from-scratch training.
weaknesses: Training compute is not matched: MoSE runs two forward/backward passes per iteration (full width plus one sampled width), so it uses more training compute than the standard MoE baseline. The paper does not control for this, so full-width improvements and frontier shifts may partly reflect extra training compute rather than the proposed architecture. No training FLOPs are reported.

Missing comparisons to existing elastic MoE methods (e.g., EMoE, RoE) and to standard MoE under matched compute (e.g., reduced-k MoE or smaller retrained MoE models). The MoE baseline is essentially a single full-width point, so the claimed shift of the compute-quality frontier is not compared against a true MoE compute-quality frontier.

No statistical significance or error bars: results appear to be single runs, and several downstream benchmarks (WSC with 273 examples, HellaSwag/PIQA/SIQA) are noisy. Differences such as WSC 0.5421 vs 0.5165 may not be significant without seeds or confidence intervals.

Potential calibration/evaluation leakage: the test-time training uses OpenWebText as the calibration stream, and OpenWebText perplexity is also reported as an evaluation metric. The paper does not specify whether calibration uses a disjoint split from evaluation; if not, in-domain results are optimistically biased.
Reproducibility is limited: the code URL is blank ('The code can be found at: .'), and key details such as calibration split, number of runs, and training FLOPs are missing.

Presentation issues: there is placeholder/duplicated text after Figure 1 ('For the real-world problem, we use the same model as the real-world problem...'), typos in equations (m vs r in Eq. 3, W_sp instead of W_up in Eq. 4), and inconsistent notation across figure captions (n16k4 vs E16A4).
The 'test-time training' is essentially a one-time calibration of a scalar gamma on a calibration set, not per-example test-time adaptation; the terminology may overstate the method's adaptivity.

Main results rely on FLOPs rather than wall-clock latency. Although Appendix B.4 provides runtime diagnostics, dynamic width execution can incur overheads not fully captured by FLOPs, so practical speedups remain somewhat uncertain.
